hook.text: For nearly forty moves, the balance refuses to break. Then the ending tilts, and every rook move starts to matter.

title: The Reykjavik Squeeze
description: Robert James Fischer and Boris Spassky meet in Game 10 of the 1972 World Championship match in Reykjavik. A quiet opening turns into central exchanges, then a rook endgame where activity means everything. Watch for the moment the balance finally tips, and for the technique that follows. This game is famous because a small edge becomes a full endgame squeeze.

The bishop retreats: {{m:7}}. Black adds a defender: {{m:8}}. White secures the king: {{m:9}}. The opening is calm, but Fischer is already preparing a central grip.

White removes a defender: {{m:43}}. Black takes it: {{m:44}}. Fischer wins more queenside space: {{m:45}}. Spassky brings a rook to the open file: {{m:46}}.
White chooses queen activity: {{m:47}}. Black invades: {{m:48}}. Fischer brings the knight back: {{m:49}}. Spassky grabs a pawn: {{m:50}}.
Fischer chooses a quiet retreat: {{m:51}}. The engine's optimism cools, and the fight is nearly level again. Black takes on the queenside: {{m:52}}. White centralizes the queen: {{m:53}}.
Spassky steadies the rook: {{m:54}}. Fischer jumps into the center: {{m:55}}. Black moves the queen away: {{m:56}}. White brings another rook into the pressure: {{m:57}}.
Black reinforces: {{m:58}}. Now Fischer starts a forcing sequence, and every capture drags another piece into the fire. First: {{m:59}}.
Spassky accepts: {{m:60}}. Fischer keeps the checks going: {{m:61}}. Black trades queens: {{m:62}}. White's knight emerges from the smoke: {{m:63}}.
Black strikes at the central rook: {{m:64}}. Fischer takes back: {{m:65}}. Spassky removes the knight: {{m:66}}. The queens are gone, and the game becomes pure technique.
White checks from the seventh rank: {{m:67}}. The king steps away: {{m:68}}. Fischer swings another rook into activity: {{m:69}}. Spassky creates counterplay: {{m:70}}.
White's king sidesteps: {{m:71}}. Black checks: {{m:72}}. Fischer gives the king room: {{m:73}}. Spassky pushes his passed pawn: {{m:74}}.

Fischer brings the king toward the center: {{m:75}}. Black looks for counterplay on the edge: {{m:76}}. White activates the rook: {{m:77}}. The balance is still delicate, but the danger signs are appearing.
Spassky invades with the rook: {{m:78}}. Fischer's king comes forward: {{m:79}}. Then Black makes the step that changes the endgame: {{m:80}}. Now White is clearly better.
Fischer does not rush. He improves the king: {{m:81}}. Spassky holds the rook line: {{m:82}}. White adds the pawn push that makes defense harder: {{m:83}}.
Black prepares a blockade: {{m:84}}. Fischer answers on the kingside: {{m:85}}. Black captures: {{m:86}}. White recaptures: {{m:87}}.

Spassky tries to lock the structure: {{m:88}}. White creates the dangerous passer: {{m:89}}. Black puts the bishop in front of the storm: {{m:90}}. The board is no longer about material alone, it is about targets.
Fischer lifts a rook into the fifth rank: {{m:91}}. Black's king tries to hold it: {{m:92}}. White takes the queenside pawn: {{m:93}}. Spassky's bishop returns to blockade: {{m:94}}.
White checks: {{m:95}}. Black centralizes the king: {{m:96}}. Fischer brings his own king closer: {{m:97}}. Spassky retreats the rook: {{m:98}}.
Now the rooks start tying Black down. White invades: {{m:99}}. Black defends: {{m:100}}. Fischer doubles the pressure: {{m:101}}.
Spassky hangs on: {{m:102}}. White keeps the rook net tight: {{m:103}}. Black returns to defense: {{m:104}}. Fischer switches sides: {{m:105}}.
Black's king lunges toward the pawns: {{m:106}}. Fischer takes the kingside pawn: {{m:107}}. Black blocks again: {{m:108}}. White pushes the passer: {{m:109}}.

Spassky's king advances, but it cannot solve the position: {{m:110}}. Fischer makes the final rook move of the game: {{m:111}}. With White ahead by far in the endgame, Spassky realized his position was lost, and resigned. This game matters because it turns a balanced middlegame into a model endgame squeeze, one small gain at a time.
